finding: Earlier parabolic-flight tests of downward burning found faster flame spread and lower limiting oxygen as gravity was reduced below Earth gravity.
quote: These results indicated increases in flame spread rates and enhanced flammability (lower limiting atmospheric oxygen content) as gravity levels were reduced from normal Earth gravity

finding: Theory comparing spread directions finds the lowest flammable oxygen percentage always occurs in concurrent (wind-aided) flow, not opposed flow.
quote: However, the lowest flammable oxygen percentage is always in the concurrent flow case.

finding: Downward flame spread rate over thin tissue was non-monotonic with gravity, peaking near Martian gravity (0.38 g) in 27.6 kPa air.
quote: The downward spread rate is non-monotonic and peaks near the Martian gravity levels of 0.38 g/gEarth.

finding: In KC-135 partial-gravity flights, upward flame spread rate over thin tissue varied linearly with gravity level for all pressures and widths tested.
quote: The upward burning spread rate varied linearly with gravity level for all pressure environments and sample widths tested

finding: A 3-D model of the limiting oxygen index (LOI) apparatus predicted lower limiting oxygen at zero gravity than at normal gravity.
quote: The LOI at normal gravity are higher than those at zero gravity for the range of forced velocity computed.

finding: The downward-spread flammability boundary versus gravity is U-shaped: extinction from short residence time at high g and radiative loss at low g.
quote: The downward spreading boundary is U-shaped showing the dual extinction limits (insufficient residence time in high g, radiative loss in low g) now predicted by several diffusion flame models.

finding: In partial-gravity flights, upward-spreading flames over thin tissue had a wider flammable domain than downward-spreading flames.
quote: The upward spreading case has a wider flammable domain that the downward case.

finding: The same model predicts the zero-gravity LOI for cotton-fiberglass is non-monotonic in forced flow, with a minimum around 5 cm/s.
quote: the LOI at zero gravity is non-monotonic and has a minimum around 5 cm/s

finding: In a 1-g low-stretch analogue, PMMA ignition delay fell threefold, so standard cone tests significantly underestimate microgravity ignition risk.
quote: For a fixed radiant flux, ignition delay times for characterization material PMMA are shown to decrease by a factor of three at low stretch, demonstrating that ignition delay times determined from normal cone tests significantly underestimate the risk in microgravity.

finding: At low stretch, as in low-gravity flows, less convective cooling lowers the critical heat flux needed for ignition.
quote: The critical heat flux for ignition is found to be lowered at low stretch as the convective cooling is reduced.

finding: NASA-STD-6001 Test 2 (standard cone) is not conservative: its buoyant flow is much stronger than in low-gravity fires.
quote: These results also demonstrate that current NASA STD 6001 Test 2 (standard cone) is not conservative since it evaluates materials flammability with a much higher inherent buoyant convective flow.

finding: At spacecraft ventilation speeds (5-20 cm/s) in microgravity, upstream (opposed-flow) flame spread was the only viable flame.
quote: Over most of the range of air ventilation rates (5-20 cm/s) comparable to spacecraft ventilation, upstream flame spread was the only viable flame.

finding: Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires, and its adequacy at lunar or Martian gravity is unknown.
quote: There is compelling evidence that the Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires, and we don't have enough information to assess if it is adequate at Lunar or Martian gravity levels.

finding: A cellulose fuel with a 16.5% O2 limiting oxygen index on Earth sustains flames at 14% O2 under spacecraft-like ventilation in microgravity.
quote: the LOI, or limiting oxygen index on Earth in opposed flow is 16.5% O2. However, if the flow is on the order of spacecraft ventilation (5-20 cm/s), flames can be sustained even at 14 % O2.

finding: KC-135 parabolic-flight experiments showed concurrent flames burn faster in partial gravity environments.
quote: Experiments conducted aboard the KC-135 [9] demonstrate the faster burning of concurrent flames in partial gravity environments.

finding: Even a very slight airflow, a fraction of a cm/s, is enough for a low-gravity flame to survive after ventilation is cut.
quote: However, experiments have shown that even a very slight air flow of a fraction of a cm/s [4] is sufficient to allow the flame to survive.

finding: At lunar and Martian gravity, buoyant flows above 20 cm/s make concurrent (Test 1-style) flame spread viable alongside opposed-flow spread.
quote: On the Moon or Mars (0.17g and 0.38 g, respectively), where buoyant flows will be greater than 20 cm/s, the concurrent flame spread will be viable simultaneously with any opposed flow flame.

finding: Under very weak ventilation, small non-luminous fingering flames can be almost undetectable yet persist for many minutes.
quote: These flames can become almost undetectable (small, non-luminous) and yet persist for many minutes [10, 11] for a fingering flame spread observed under very weak ventilation.

finding: Raising the flow 100-fold to 50 cm/s did not blow out a tiny fingering flame; it flared into a much larger spreading flame.
quote: When the flow was turned up 100-fold to 50 cm/s, the flame did not blow out as one would expect, but flared up into a much larger spreading flame.

finding: A material that passes NASA's upward Test 1 would most likely not burn in quiescent (no-flow) microgravity.
quote: A material that passes this test would most likely not burn in a quiescent microgravity environment

finding: For some materials the most flammable condition is at very low flow velocities, below those produced by upward burning in normal gravity.
quote: The most flammable condition for some materials is at very low velocities, below those for upward spread in normal gravity

finding: In reduced gravity, the suppressant agent concentration needed to extinguish flames rose as airflow velocity increased, up to about 10 cm/s.
quote: In reduced gravity, the agent concentration required to suppress the flames increased as the velocity increased, up to approximately 10 cm/s (the maximum velocity evaluated in this experiment).

finding: At 10 cm/s airflow in low gravity, the suppressant effective enthalpy needed to extinguish flames was about the same as in normal gravity.
quote: The effective enthalpy required to extinguish flames at velocities of 10 cm/s is approximately the same as the concentrations in normal gravity.

finding: The ISS uses CO2 as its fire suppressant, with requirements developed from terrestrial NFPA 12 regulations.
quote: Carbon Dioxide is the current suppressant of choice on the ISS. The requirements were developed based on NFPA 12 Regulations

finding: Shuttle smoke experiments found larger smoke particles in some low-gravity cases, and ISS and Shuttle smoke detectors performed differently in low gravity.
quote: Recent space shuttle experiments confirmed that, in some cases, increased particles sizes are seen in low-gravity and that the relative performance of the ISS (International Space Station) and space-shuttle smoke-detectors changes in low-gravity

finding: DAFT found the ISS cabin very clean, with background particulate far below the Space Shuttle and ground environments, critical data for future detector design.
quote: These background levels are critical to the design of future smoke detectors. The ISS cabin was found to be a very clean environment with particulate levels substantially below the space shuttle and typical ground-based environments.

finding: The Shuttle CSD experiment demonstrated that spacecraft smoke detector design must be based on low-gravity smoke data.
quote: Smoke detector design must be based on low-g data

finding: Lowering cabin pressure to 58.6 kPa while keeping 21% O2 shortened PMMA's piloted ignition time by 17% on average.
quote: It was found that reducing the pressure while keeping the oxygen concentration at 21% reduced the ignition time by 17% on average.

finding: Ignition tests at standard atmospheric conditions will underpredict how readily spacecraft materials ignite in the planned exploration atmosphere.
quote: These results show that tests conducted in standard atmospheric conditions will underpredict the ignition of materials intended for use on spacecraft

finding: The critical heat flux needed to ignite a material in microgravity could be as low as half the value measured in normal gravity.
quote: Additionally, the critical heat flux (CHF) for ignition in microgravity could be reduced as much as half of the value determined in normal gravity.

finding: Earlier studies agree that in the low-speed flows typical of spacecraft, piloted ignition delays are shorter than in normal-gravity buoyant flows.
quote: in the low velocity flows commonly encountered in space-based facilities, piloted ignition delay times are shorter than those in the buoyancy-induced flows of normal gravity

finding: In a space exploration atmosphere (58.6 kPa, 32% O2), PMMA's piloted ignition delay was 27% shorter on average than at standard sea-level conditions.
quote: In SEA, the ignition delay time decreases 27% on average compared to standard atmospheric conditions.

finding: Many materials used on the Shuttle or ISS are only tested and rated to 30% O2 at 10.2 psia, the brief pre-EVA atmosphere.
quote: Many of the materials now used in the Shuttle or on ISS are therefore only tested and rated to 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia.

material: Nomex HT90-40 fabric, Ultem 1000 film, Mylar G film
finding: In drop-tower microgravity with ventilation-like flow, three spacecraft materials burned at lower oxygen than their NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 limits, by up to 4% O2.
quote: the fuels burned in 0g at lower oxygen concentrations than they did using the NASA Standard 6001 Test 1 protocol

finding: In drop-tower microgravity with 30 cm/s concurrent flow at 10.2 psia, Mylar G film kept burning at 17% O2, below its 20.8% 1-g limiting index.
In drop-tower microgravity with 30 cm/s concurrent flow at 14.7 psia, Nomex HT90-40 kept burning at 23% O2, below its 25.4% 1-g limiting index.
In 1-g upward Test 1 data, Mylar G film's upward limiting oxygen index is 20.8% O2 at 10.2 psia, with a 20% maximum oxygen concentration.
quote: Mylar G 20.8% O2, 10.2 psia* 20% O2, 10.2 psia*

finding: In 1-g upward Test 1 data, Nomex HT90-40 fabric's upward limiting oxygen index is 25.4% O2 at 14.7 psia, with a 22% maximum oxygen concentration.
quote: Nomex HT90-40 fabric 25.4% O2 (±0.6), 14.7 psia* 22% O2, 14.7 psia*

finding: In microgravity, Ultem film's mean flammability limit drops to 22.5% O2, inside the Shuttle/ISS nominal atmosphere range, so it could burn if ignited.
quote: However, in 0g the mean flammability limit is 22.5%, which falls within the nominal range for the atmosphere, indicating the material could burn if ignited.

finding: In 1 g, Ultem film's mean flammability limit is 25.25% O2, at least 2.25 points above the Shuttle and ISS nominal 21% ± 2% atmosphere.
quote: In 1g, the mean flammability limit for Ultem is 25.25%, which is at least 2.25% above the nominal range for the atmosphere.

finding: Along the normoxic curve, opposed flame spread over thin cellulose in microgravity rises from about 1 to 5 cm/s as O2 increases from 21% to 80%.
quote: Opposed (or upwind) spread increases from about 1 to 5 cm/s as percent O2 goes from 21 to 80%.

finding: Analysis suggests the 1-g upward flammability limit (MOC) from Test 1 is essentially dictated by the critical heat flux for ignition.
quote: We propose that the upward flammability limit (1g MOC) derived from Test 1 is essentially a limit dictated by the critical heat flux for ignition

finding: Correlations from drop-tower data show opposed (upwind) flame spread is faster than concurrent spread across nearly all spacecraft atmospheres and ventilation flows, especially normoxic ones.
quote: over virtually the entire range of spacecraft atmospheres and flow conditions, the opposed spread is faster in microgravity, especially for the normoxic case.

finding: In 99.8% oxygen, Orion crew-module materials may burn at total pressures as low as 0.4 psia, so pressure must stay below that for self-extinguishment.
quote: The results show that CEV CM materials may be flammable in oxygen at pressures as low as 0.4 psia and that the pressure should be kept below 0.4 psia to ensure they are still self-extinguishing.

finding: The pressure flammability threshold in oxygen was far lower than expected; the standard Test 1 chemical igniter itself would not burn below 0.7 psia.
quote: this pressure threshold is appreciably lower than had been expected based on general testing experience, including the failure of the standard chemical igniter to burn below 0.7 psia

material: Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, Pyrell
finding: On ISS, most smoke particles from overheated spacecraft materials averaged 200-400 nm, but quiescent cases produced some substantially larger particles.
quote: Overall the majority of the average smoke particle sizes were found to be in the 200 nm to 400 nm range with the quiescent cases producing some cases with substantially larger particles.

finding: Smoke particles grew larger at low flow rates, so smoke trapped in avionics enclosures should be substantially larger than smoke in ventilated areas.
quote: These figures show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow rates. This indicates that smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.

finding: SAME-R results suggest spacecraft smoke detectors must measure more than one moment of the particle size distribution to pick smoke out from background.
quote: This suggests that detection of these particles against the background environment will require a detection system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution.

finding: SAME-R's two-moment MPASS prototype could distinguish a strong signal from dense smoke from one caused by fewer, very large dust particles.
quote: The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles

finding: Martian-gravity drop-tower tests suggest a gravity level below Earth's exists at which materials burn more readily than on Earth.
quote: the data presented in this paper for Martian gravity suggest that there is a gravity level below Earth’s at which materials burn more readily than on Earth.

finding: In low gravity, anything that restricts free oxygen flow past a burning sample, such as edge curling or swelling, reduces its flammability.
quote: Since oxygen transport is critical to low gravity flames, anything that reduces the free flow of oxygen past the sample will reduce the material’s flammability.

finding: For Mylar, Ultem and Nomex, 1-g flammability limits were generally not conservative: reduced-gravity limits were up to 5.75% oxygen lower.
quote: As shown in Fig. 6 and Table I, the 1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials as evidenced by the negative ∆O2%, by up to -5.75% oxygen.

finding: For charring Nomex and Ultem, the oxygen safety margin at 0 g (30 cm/s concurrent flow) was close to zero relative to 1 g.
quote: For these charring materials, the oxygen margin of safety in 0g is very close to zero, indicating that any reduced charring for 0g may be offset by less heat release in the reduced convective environment.

finding: For charring fuels (Nomex, Ultem), the oxygen margin of safety at lunar gravity was about 2.5% oxygen below 1 g.
quote: In Lunar gravity, the oxygen margin of safety for these charring fuels is ~ 2.5% lower than 1g.

finding: Mylar's limiting oxygen versus gravity level is bounded by two U-shaped curves: flames survive only within a range of g-levels.
quote: The two u-shaped curves are presumed to bound the flammability boundary of this material.

finding: For non-charring Mylar, the lack of gravity-driven dripping keeps molten fuel in the flame zone, giving a 4-5% oxygen negative safety margin.
quote: the absence of gravitational-induced dripping keeps heated molten fuel in the flame zone rather than removing it, and the result is a significantly negative oxygen margin of safety (~4-5%) in Martian, Lunar, and 0g.

finding: Consistently negative safety margins suggest 1-g flammability screening may not be conservative: some materials rated safe for space may actually be flammable.
quote: normal gravity material flammability screening tests may not be conservative and some materials tested to be safe for use in space may actually be flammable.

finding: With the same 10 cm/s concurrent flow in normal gravity, the SIBAL fabric flame kept growing in size and spread rate.
quote: 1-g with flow (10 cm/s) Growing flame size and spread

finding: At 10 cm/s concurrent flow in microgravity, the SIBAL fabric flame reached a steady size and spread rate.
quote: Comparison of 0-g and 1-g Concurrent Flow Flames 0-g with flow (10 cm/s) Steady flame size and spread

finding: In normal gravity, a flame on the SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric does not propagate downward.
quote: 1-g Flame does not propagate downward

finding: In microgravity opposed flow, SIBAL flames reached steady spread at each flow speed, spreading fastest at an intermediate flow speed.
quote: For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed.

finding: Lowering concurrent airflow to about 1 cm/s in microgravity caused quenching extinction of the burning cotton-fiberglass fabric.
quote: In addition, by decreasing concurrent flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s), quenching extinction was observed.

finding: BASS showed enhanced microgravity flammability for opposed-flow spread over SIBAL fabric, which self-extinguishes when spreading downward in normal-gravity air.
quote: These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread).

finding: The authors propose rating materials safe only above their 1-g normoxic limiting pressure plus a roughly 10 kPa safety factor for enhanced spacecraft flammability.
quote: we can define the material as being safe to use at the NULP + SF (where SF is on the order of 10 kPa, based on existing flammability data)

finding: Test 1's 25-second igniter can under-heat thick samples, so materials thicker than about 3 mm may pass by failing to ignite rather than by being truly non-flammable.
quote: It is thus possible to pass Test 1 with a material that is thick enough so that the observed limit is actually an ignition limit, and not a flammability limit.

finding: In 1-g tests, Nomex HT90-40's normoxic upward limiting pressure is about 90 kPa: below that cabin pressure, at constant O2 partial pressure, it is flammable.
quote: Published data [17] for Nomex HT-90-40 indicates that the NULP in 1g is approximately 90 kPa for the concurrent vertical worst case test geometry, most similar to NASA’s Test 1.

finding: Proposed screening: run Test 1 first at the lowest planned cabin pressure, the 8.2 psia exploration atmosphere; passing there implies safety at all higher normoxic pressures.
quote: So it makes sense to start at the lowest expected total pressure for a spacecraft (8.2 psia exploration atmosphere, excluding EVA environments which are a special case), and run constant partial pressure of oxygen Test 1 tests there.

finding: At a fixed oxygen partial pressure, spacecraft materials are most flammable at the lowest total pressure, which means the highest oxygen percentage.
quote: The general trend for all these materials shown in Figures 7-8 is for flammability to be worst at the lower total pressures for fixed partial pressure of O2, which corresponds to the highest % O2.

finding: In BASS-II opposed-flow tests on ISS, flame spread along PMMA rods was not observed below 16.4% O2.
quote: This is consistent with tests for opposed flow flame spread rods that were also done as part of BASS-II [18], where flame spread was not observed below 16.4 % O2.

finding: Because the BASS-II blowoff boundary is linear, extrapolating it to zero flow could be used to de-rate materials tested in normal gravity so they will not burn in space.
quote: This will allow us to de-rate materials based on normal gravity flammability tests to ensure the material will not burn in space.

finding: BASS-II PMMA rods burned down to 13.6% O2; extrapolating the linear blowoff boundary to zero stretch gives 13.3% O2, a slightly more conservative floor.
quote: Using the y-intercept of the linear fit (13.3 % O2 in the Figure 4 fit, versus the minimum test point of 13.6 % O2) would add a slight level of conservatism.

finding: Adding a forced upward airflow made silicone more flammable in 1-g upward tests than buoyant flow alone.
quote: Upward tests in air with an added forced flow were more flammable.

finding: In 1-g tests, 0.25 and 0.36 mm silicone sheets burned farther with the flame spreading downward than upward.
quote: The 0.25-mm- and 0.36-mm-thick samples had a greater burn length in the downward configuration than their corresponding upward cases.

finding: In every oxygen atmosphere tested, silicone that could be ignited in the downward configuration burned the entire sample length.
quote: In all atmospheres tested, if the silicone could be ignited in the downward configuration then it would burn the entire length of the sample.

finding: On ISS, a flame over 0.1 mm PMMA sheet approached blowoff extinction as the flow speed crossed 40 cm/s.
quote: Flame nearing blow off extinction as the flow velocity crosses 40 cm/s.

finding: On ISS, a flame over 0.1 mm PMMA sheet quenched radiatively once the opposing flow fell below 2 cm/s.
quote: Sequence of top views showing radiative quenching when flow velocity goes below 2 cm/s.

finding: PMMA rods in ISS low-speed flows spread flames more slowly than the same rods burning in 1-g natural convection; spread also slowed with larger diameter.
quote: There is a downward trend in flame spread rate as sample diameter increases for both the 1g and μg (microgravity) tests. 1g tests have higher flame spread rates than μg.

finding: On ISS, a 1/4-inch PMMA rod spread steadily at 13.6% O2, whereas in 1 g the same rod blows off at 16% O2.
quote: The 1g blowoff for the ¼” rod is at 16% oxygen, whereas we obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen in BASS-II.

finding: BASS-II located the minimum-oxygen point of PMMA's flammability boundary at very low flow speeds, comparable to diffusive flows.
quote: The minimum in the flammability boundary is at low speed, on the order of diffusive flows.

finding: BASS-II gave PMMA a negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4% O2, so normal-gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.
quote: Thus the material has a negative Oxygen Margin of Safety of 2.4% O2, and the normal gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.

finding: On ISS, a SIBAL fabric flame at 1 atm and 18.7% O2, ignited at 5 cm/s, quenched as the concurrent flow was gradually reduced to 2.2 cm/s.
quote: Top view of a typical quenching time sequence. 2.2-cm wide SIBAL fabric sample in 1 atm. and 18.7% O2. Ignited at 5 cm/s flow at right end, then reduced to 2.2 cm/s gradually.

finding: In normal-gravity wind-tunnel tests, PMMA rods repeatedly blew off at 14% O2 rather than sustaining a flame.
quote: Unlike in the 1g setup in the lab, the rod blew off in repeated tests at 14% oxygen in the larger wind tunnel as shown in Figure 4.

finding: Extrapolating normal-gravity PMMA rod blowoff limits to zero stretch predicts 13.4% O2 as the floor below which the fuel cannot burn at any flow.
quote: which estimates that 13.4% O2 is the limiting oxygen concentration below which the fuel cannot burn at any stretch rate

finding: SoFIE researchers propose de-rating materials by a negative oxygen margin of safety; for PMMA rods it is 1.4% O2.
quote: Negative Oxygen Margin of Safety to de-rate materials. PMMA rods: NOMS = 1.4% O2

finding: Even in 1-g testing, few thin-sheet materials are rated for the 34% O2, 8.2 psia exploration atmosphere.
quote: Thin fuel sheets: few materials rated even in 1g at 34% O2, 8.2 psia (exploration atmosphere).

finding: Modeled thin PMMA flames in microgravity quench radiatively below 2 cm/s airflow and approach blowoff extinction above 40 cm/s.
quote: radiative quenching when flow velocity goes below 2 cm/s. Right: Flame nearing blow off extinction as the flow velocity crosses 40 cm/s.

finding: BASS-II's low-speed microgravity fires burned inefficiently, with CO-to-CO2 ratios an order of magnitude higher than efficient flue gases.
quote: The CO to CO2 ratios for these fires are an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases, indicating that these flames are not efficient.

finding: In BASS-II, flames spread faster on two-sided than one-sided PMMA samples, and thicker fuels spread more slowly.
quote: In general, the flames spread faster for two-sided burns compared to one-sided burns. The greater the thickness of the fuel, the greater is the time taken for the flame to spread and so the lower is the spread rate.

finding: On ISS, PMMA rods took up to 230 s to ignite near the limit, so Test 1's fixed ~25 s igniter may be testing ignitability rather than flammability.
quote: Successful ignitions occur in nondimensional ignitable region, and with ignition delay times as long as 230 s. NASA Test 1 25-s ignition time may be too short for flammability test and so may be an ignition test.

finding: BASS-II's PMMA-rod flammability boundary bottoms out near 13.5% O2 at low stretch rates of 8–12 per second, as theory predicted.
quote: The minimum in this boundary occurs at a = 8 to 12 s–1 at approximately 13.5 percent O2, in good agreement with the predicted a at the minima in the flammability boundary

finding: For the BASS-II PMMA rods, the normal-gravity upward limiting oxygen concentration used for comparison is 15.4% O2.
quote: The normal-gravity upward limiting O2 concentration of 15.4 percent O2 (Ref. 23) is plotted for comparison

finding: In purely forced concurrent flow on ISS, flames over thin SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric quenched at low flow speeds between 1 and 5 cm/s.
quote: The quenching velocities are small (between 1 and 5 cm/s), and an accurate determination is necessary to resolve the slope of the quenching boundary.

finding: Saffire IV-V fires releasing up to 10 kW measurably affected Cygnus cabin pressure, temperature and CO2, but average vehicle conditions stayed acceptable.
quote: The fire events had a measurable impact on the vehicle pressure, temperature, and carbon dioxide concentration. However, despite having heat release rates up to 10 kW, the average vehicle conditions did not rise to unacceptable levels.

finding: Reducing airflow to a low value, rather than stopping it, can extinguish low-gravity fires faster through convective cooling.
quote: Furthermore, using reduced air flow rather than going to zero air flow can lead to more rapid extinction due to the convective cooling.

finding: Stopping airflow does not guarantee quick extinction in low gravity; thin materials, higher oxygen and heated fuel can all support extended burning.
quote: These results indicate that extinction of the fire cannot be assumed to occur quickly under quiescent conditions. Thin materials, higher oxygen concentrations and heating of the solid fuel can all support extended burning.

finding: Without buoyancy to carry hot fuel vapors away, as in normal gravity, those vapors accumulate more easily in low gravity.
quote: Unlike in normal gravity where buoyancy tends to move hot vapors away from the source, in low gravity hot fuel vapors can more easily accumulate.

finding: In orbit, concurrent flames over thin fabrics reached a limiting size, unlike normal-gravity upward flames, which tend to grow continuously.
quote: concurrent flames spreading over thin fuels will achieve a limiting size. This behavior contrasts with normal gravity upward spread where flames tend to grow continuously.

finding: Thick PMMA slabs burning in orbit reached an upper flame-length limit, whereas similar 1-g tests did not reach a steady length.
quote: In all these cases the flame length reached an upper limit contrary to similar 1-g tests that did not reach a steady length.

finding: The Saffire V-3 flame grew longer than the other samples, attributed to its enhanced oxygen concentration, which is expected to reduce flame standoff distance.
quote: Increasing the ambient oxygen concentration can be expected to reduce the standoff distance. Consequently, the final length of the Saffire V-3 flame is greater than the other samples due to the enhanced oxygen concentration.

finding: NASA-STD-6001 tests the worst-case, usually thinnest, sample; Saffire results indicate relatively thin surface structures must also be considered.
quote: NASA STD 6001 requires testing with the worst case (usually the thinnest) sample. These results indicate that relatively thin surface structures must be considered.

finding: Low-gravity ignition is likely easiest at low airflow; higher flow velocities delay or deter ignition through heat losses from the fuel surface.
quote: The most ignitable condition is likely to be at low flow rates since as the flow velocity increases, ignition becomes delayed or deterred due to heat losses from the surface of the fuel the adjacent flow.

finding: Thick-fuel flame growth in orbit differed from NASA-STD-6001 Test 1; this does not invalidate the test but affects how its results are interpreted.
quote: Thick fuel flame growth was found to be dissimilar from that seen in NASA STD 6001 Test 1. This does not invalidate the test but does affect the interpretation of the test results

finding: HCl interacts strongly with aluminum, so acid gas released in the Cygnus cabin may adsorb onto surfaces before reaching far-field sensors.
quote: HCl interacts strongly with aluminum and oxidized aluminum, so acid may be adsorbing onto cabin surfaces prior to reaching the FFD

finding: Particle mass in smoke from all five Saffire IV-V burns was dominated by submicron (PM1) particles.
quote: Particle mass concentration dominated by submicron particles (PM1) in all five burn events

finding: Saffire IV-V particle sizes and mass concentrations per fuel could feed smoke emission factors that better predict spacecraft smoke-detector alarm times.
quote: Particle sizes and mass concentrations from combusting different fuels could be used in future modeling studies to generate smoke emission factors to better predict times to alarm for spacecraft smoke detectors

finding: Both 1-g experiments and FDS simulations show concurrent flame spread over thin cotton fabric slows as ambient pressure is reduced.
quote: It is shown that as ambient pressure is reduced the flame spread rate over a thin fabric is also reduced, both experimentally and numerically.

finding: Simulations indicate low pressure and low gravity reduce buoyancy differently, so results from one should not be assumed to transfer to the other.
quote: These results may indicate another aspect in which reduced buoyant flows (gravity and pressure) may differ and caution should be exercised when extrapolating results from one to the other condition.

finding: Microgravity pyrolysis lengths, from cotton simulations and Saffire-II SIBAL flight data, were well below any low-pressure case tested or simulated at 1 g.
quote: cotton modeling results or experiments for Sibal (Saffire -II) for microgravity appear significantly lower than any low pressure case tested or simulated at 1 g.

finding: FDS simulations show that lowering either pressure or gravity reduces convective heating of the fabric ahead of the flame, slowing concurrent spread.
quote: as the pressure (top row) and gravity level (bottom row) are reduced independently, the convective heat flux to the solid surface is also reduced

finding: Normal-gravity MOC data show raising oxygen concentration affects flammability much more than raising pressure, similarly across materials.
quote: The nearly vertical lines for the pressure vs. MOC show that increasing oxygen has a significantly greater effect than increasing pressure

finding: Drop-tower centrifuge data show the oxygen level at which materials self-extinguish (MOC) can be lower at lunar gravity than at zero or Martian gravity.
quote: Lunar-g MOC can be lower than either zero- or Martian-g levels

finding: In partial-gravity drop-tower tests, Nomex, Mylar and Ultem flames all propagated at the oxygen level where they self-extinguish in normal gravity.
quote: Partial-g flames propagated at the normal-g MOC for all materials (charring and non-charring)

finding: In partial gravity, smoke transport for fire detection involves a competition between smoke production rate, buoyancy and ventilation air circulation.
quote: In partial-g, there will be a competition between rate of smoke production, buoyancy, and ECLSS air circulation

finding: Models show that in zero gravity with forced ventilation, the spacecraft volume must reach alarm-level smoke before a detector alarm sounds.
quote: Modeling has shown that in zero-g with forced convection, the spacecraft volume must reach the alarm level before an alarm will sound

finding: Theory and experiments indicate oxygen flammability limits at lunar gravity are lower than those measured at 1 g.
quote: Theory and experimental results indicate that oxygen flammability limits in lunar-g are lower than those measured in 1-g

finding: Turning off cabin ventilation to starve a fire is not effective at lunar gravity, because buoyancy still drives flow.
quote: Turning the ECLSS flow off to extinguish a fire in lunar-g is not effective because the reduced gravity will still induce buoyant flow velocities

finding: On ISS, flames over 12.7-mm PMMA rods in microgravity were weaker but still propagated, and at lower oxygen than in 1 g.
quote: The microgravity flame is weaker but can still propagate and at lower %O2 than in 1-g

finding: SIBAL fabric 2.2 cm wide supports both concurrent and opposed-flow spread in microgravity, but downward (opposed) spread cannot be achieved on Earth.
quote: In microgravity, both concurrent and opposed-flow flame spread are possible, but on Earth, downward flame spread (opposed flow) cannot be achieved. This demonstrates enhanced flammability in microgravity, and suggests similar behavior at partial gravity.

finding: Theory and experiments show some materials that will not burn at 1 g will burn at 0 g with low-speed flow, or at lunar gravity.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

finding: A model shows the oxygen concentration needed for flammability reaches its minimum near lunar gravity.
quote: Oxygen concentration for flammability reaches a minimum value in the vicinity of g = gMoon (left; model)

finding: FLEX methanol droplets showed diffusive extinction from water absorption and radiative extinction, with a limiting oxygen index near 12-13% at atmospheric pressure.
quote: Diffusive extinction due to water absorption, and radiative extinction were observed. The limiting oxygen index (LOI) ~ 12-13% oxygen at atmospheric pressure.

finding: Widely used detailed chemical kinetic models fail to accurately predict the second-stage cool-flame extinction observed in FLEX and need improvement.
quote: Existing, widely-used detailed chemical kinetic models do not accurately predict the 2nd stage cool flame extinction (and warm flame) and need further improvement

finding: Cool flames seen in FLEX produce partially oxidized fuel and can potentially re-ignite into hot flames, a fire safety concern for spacecraft.
quote: These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments

finding: In Saffire VI-3, far-field smoke reached a tight 1 mg/m3 alarm threshold only at 981 s, after much of the hazardous gas release.
quote: Selecting 1 mg/m3 as a relatively tight alarm threshold, the FFD detector reached that threshold at 981 seconds. By this point, much of the hazardous gas release had occurred.

finding: Both Saffire VI PMMA fires pushed cabin CO2 past its allowable level and CO well above the 24-hour limit, near the 1-hour limit.
quote: the allowable CO2 level was exceeded by both of the PMMA tests on Saffire VI. For carbon monoxide the levels were well above the 24-hour SMAC and quite close to the 1-hour level.

finding: Saffire VI showed that, as in terrestrial fires, smoke and gaseous products rather than heat are the main crew hazard of a spacecraft fire.
quote: the human hazard from a fire in a spacecraft is very similar to terrestrial fires where the heat from the fire is not the principal hazard and rather the smoke and gaseous products are a much greater concern.

finding: In ground (1-g) tests, SIBAL fabric burned downward with a bright flame in 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi.
quote: A bright flame burns SIBAL fuel downwards in 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi

finding: FM2 drop-tower centrifuge tests (5.18 s) give increasing evidence that materials have lower oxygen flammability limits at lunar than at Earth gravity.
quote: Provides Increasing evidence that materials have lower oxygen limits of flammability in Lunar gravity than in Earth gravity according to the 5.18 second tests using the zero-gravity drop facility.

finding: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric burns downward in air at lunar gravity (centrifuge and parabolic tests), yet extinguishes immediately after ignition at Earth gravity.
quote: SIBAL fabric has been found to only burn downward in air in lunar gravity (via Lunar gravity centrifuge and parabolic flight) where on Earth’s gravity it extinguishes immediately after ignition.

finding: A crew-cabin fire model calibrated on large-scale exploration-atmosphere tests predicted substantially higher cabin air temperatures at lunar gravity than at 1 g.
quote: Air temperature in the lunar-g simulation was substantially higher than in 1-g showing buoyant transport significantly affects habitability

finding: LUCI showed that material flammability testing at partial gravity is feasible on a spinning suborbital vehicle (Blue Origin New Shepard).
quote: The LUCI scientific objectives were achieved. Material flammability testing at partial-g is feasible using a spinning vehicle.

finding: A 4-mm PMMA rod burning upward in air in simulated lunar gravity grew until its flame engulfed the entire rod.
quote: PMMA rod burning upward in air in Lunar-g, 30 s after ignition. The flame eventually grows to engulf the entire rod.

finding: On LUCI's spinning rocket, the Coriolis force pulled the PMMA flame away from the fuel axis, which was aligned with the centrifugal acceleration.
quote: The one on the right demonstrates how the Coriolis force pulls the flame away from the axis of the fuel, which is aligned with the direction of the centrifugal acceleration.

finding: In LUCI, cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) fabric flames went out about 45 s later in simulated lunar gravity than in the 1-g comparison burn.
quote: 1-g extinction happens ~ 45 seconds sooner than partial-g extinction

finding: In 1-g flow-tunnel tests, imposed flow had negligible effect on Nomex flame length and spread, likely because buoyancy outweighed the imposed flow.
quote: Flow rate has negligible effect on flame length and flame spread over the tested range. Likely due to the buoyant force outweighing the imposed flow

finding: Nomex HT90-40 fabric needed more oxygen to burn at lunar gravity (~29%) and 0 g (~38%) than at 1 g (~23%).
quote: Limiting oxygen concentrations (LOC): o 1G ~23% Oxygen o Lunar-G ~29% Oxygen o 0G ~38% Oxygen

finding: In 1-g flow-tunnel tests of Nomex HT90-40 at 8.2 psi, higher oxygen concentration increased flame length and tip spread rate.
quote: Oxygen concentration is observed to increase flame length and tip spread rate.

finding: Flame spread rate peaks near lunar gravity, so early numerical and experimental evidence suggested the Moon could be more hazardous.
quote: Early numerical and experimental evidence suggested that Lunar gravity could be more hazardous, since flame spread rate as a function of gravity peaks there [2].

finding: The minimum oxygen concentration needed for flammability is lowest near lunar gravity.
quote: Related work suggests that oxygen concentration for flammability reaches a minimum value in the vicinity of g = g Lunar.

finding: Some materials that will not burn in 1 g will burn at lunar gravity, or in 0 g with a low-speed flow.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

finding: KC-135 experiments found downward flame spread rate peaks at partial gravity.
quote: Downward flame spread rate peaks in partial-g [right, Sacksteder; KC-135 experiments].

finding: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable gravity condition.
quote: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

finding: Higher oxygen concentration or higher oxygen partial pressure generally means higher material flammability risk in crew cabins.
quote: Generally, higher oxygen concentrations and/or higher oxygen partial pressures equate to a higher flammability risk.

finding: Although ISS runs near 21% O2, its onboard materials have historically been tested only up to a 30% maximum oxygen concentration at sea-level pressure.
quote: While the International Space Station operates around 21% oxygen, historically materials used onboard have been tested up to a maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) of 30% at sea level pressure

finding: Materials intended for the 34% O2 Artemis cabin atmosphere have typically been flammability-tested up to 37% O2 to cover control error bands.
quote: Materials to be used in the 34% atmosphere, have typically been tested up to a 37% oxygen concentration for the reasons mentioned above.

finding: Weaker buoyant flow on the Moon means a material that self-extinguishes by blowoff in Earth gravity may keep burning in lunar gravity.
quote: This effect occurs more readily on Earth because the higher gravity causes higher flow velocities. Thus, a material that self-extinguishes in Earth gravity may continue to burn in lunar gravity.

finding: In microgravity a smouldering fire may not spread without cabin ventilation, because airflow must supply the oxygen needed for propagation.
quote: since airflow is needed to sustain a minimum oxygen concentration for propagation, a smouldering flame in microgravity may not propogate in the absence of cabin ventilation

finding: Recent testing found very few textiles can pass NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 at 37% O2 and 8.2 psia.
quote: Overall, recent testing revealed very few textiles capable of passing NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, the standard NASA test for flammability, at 37% O2 and 8.2 psia

finding: Keeping O2 partial pressure up in a low-pressure cabin means raising O2 concentration, which makes materials more flammable.
quote: A consequence of raising O2 concentration to sustain O2 partial pressure in a low-pressure environment is that the flammability of materials increases with increasing O2 concentration.

finding: Fewer materials qualify in higher-O2 cabins, a significant challenge for spacecraft design and operations.
quote: The reduction in the number of candidate materials that can be used in higher O2 environments represents a significant challenge in designing and operating a spacecraft.

finding: NASA has limited material flammability data above 30% O2.
quote: However, NASA has limited material flammability data at O2 concentration higher than 30% (F-12a).

finding: Flame Design tested the hypothesis that microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when their peak temperature first falls below 1130 K.
quote: Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K.

finding: SAME-R's record says its results can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future long-duration spacecraft missions.
quote: the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions.

finding: SAME's hypothesis: changed smoke size distribution and number density will affect smoke detector response, possibly leaving some detectors silent.
quote: The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

finding: SAME tested the hypothesis that liquid aerosol smoke produced in microgravity has substantially larger droplets than smoke produced under the same conditions in normal gravity.
quote: it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity

finding: PSI-115 hypothesized that without buoyancy, reduced mixing and heat transfer alter combustion-vapor history and particle trajectories, changing smoke composition.
quote: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke.

finding: PSI-142 found the flammable region of warm and cool flames expands at elevated pressures, due to increased low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity.
quote: At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure.

finding: CFI-G set out to show in flight cool diffusion flames that extinguish when flow rate drops but transition to hot flames when it rises.
quote: Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

material: BRE gas burner emulating condensed fuels
finding: BRE observed quasi-steady burning emulating materials like PMMA and nylon in microgravity with no airflow, though shutting off ventilation is an established step against spacecraft fires.
quote: Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires.

material: BRE gas burner emulating condensed fuels
finding: In BRE, combustion continued without airflow in elevated-oxygen atmospheres that are being considered for future spacecraft.
quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft

material: BRE gas burner emulating condensed fuels
finding: In BRE, flames burning without airflow in a normal 21% oxygen atmosphere self-extinguished in a short time.
quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

finding: Preliminary BRE results suggest NASA may want to use its cone-calorimeter flammability Test 2 more, since it measures properties matching the microgravity flames observed.
quote: they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

finding: BASS-II's record says its results help engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods for future space missions.
quote: BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions.

finding: BASS-II tested the hypothesis that materials in ventilated microgravity burn as well as, or better than, the same materials in normal gravity.
quote: BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical

finding: BASS-II's record says NASA's normal-gravity upward-burning test, considered worst case on Earth, may not be conservative for flammability in space.
quote: using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space.

finding: BASS notes that testing all but the thinnest materials needs longer microgravity time than drop towers or parabolic aircraft provide.
quote: To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.

finding: BASS used nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity, which its record links directly to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
quote: Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.

finding: DAFT/DAFT-2 tested whether a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.
quote: DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

finding: DAFT's record states that longer missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with greater reliability and sensitivity.
quote: Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity.

finding: PSI-62 hypothesized its unsteady flamelet-manifold model could reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone.
quote: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone

finding: FLEX tested whether the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity significantly changes flammability limits and fire-suppressant efficacy compared with normal gravity.
quote: Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions.

finding: FLEX's record says its microgravity findings on CO2, helium and SF6 suppressants can lead to more efficient, less harmful fire suppression systems.
quote: The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events.

finding: Saffire's premise: because fire behaves very differently in normal and reduced gravity, designing spacecraft fire safety from terrestrial fires and standards carries inherent risk.
quote: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle

finding: Saffire results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials and help validate NASA's material selection criteria.
quote: Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size.
